# Writing (signs that record language) (`writing_invention`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Core idea: Fixed visible signs stand for words of a spoken language, so a message can be read by someone absent or born later. Writing was invented independently at least three times (Mesopotamia, China, Mesoamerica; Egypt possibly a fourth). At Uruk, early tablets combine numerals with signs for goods; early Shang inscriptions record royal divination. One way to extend a script is the rebus principle: a sign for a word is reused for its sound, so names and any sentence can be written ('bee' + 'leaf' for 'belief'). A working system needs a fixed sign list, phonetic use of signs, a cheap durable medium (clay, papyrus, bamboo, bark paper) and people who know its conventions.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking writing was invented once and spread: Chinese and Maya writing are independent inventions
  - Calling any picture or tally 'writing': without a link to the words of a language it records only a few fixed meanings
  - Assuming early writing was for literature or religion: in Mesopotamia about 85–90 % of the earliest tablets are administrative accounts
  - Treating the token-to-tablet origin theory (Schmandt-Besserat) as settled fact: it is influential but disputed in detail
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3350–3200 BC – proto-cuneiform accounting tablets at Uruk; by c. 2600 BC cuneiform writes Sumerian sentences and literature; egypt: c. 3250 BC – inscribed labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (dating and independence from Mesopotamia disputed); hieroglyphs fully developed by c. 2700 BC; india: c. 2600–1900 BC – Indus signs on seals, undeciphered; whether they are full writing is disputed; china: c. 1250 BC – Shang oracle-bone inscriptions at Anyang, already a mature script ancestral to modern characters; greece: c. 1450–1400 BC – Linear B, a syllabary for Mycenaean Greek, adapted from Minoan Linear A; americas: c. 300 BC – Maya glyphs at San Bartolo (Guatemala); earlier Olmec and Zapotec signs (Cascajal block c. 900 BC) are disputed
- Read:
  - Peter T. Daniels & William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
  - Andrew Robinson, The Story of Writing (1995)
  - Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing (1992)
